title: 📖 06 — Politics, Factions & Institutions
rawNotionMarkup: Edition II continuity and provenance note. Complete available Notion topic reference retained without compression; editorial guardrails and historically distinct detail appear below. Not final until the ChatGPT export is compared. Creator revisions remain authoritative. ## Edition II continuity guardrails - The Seven Khazari Thrones are independent; the Eldar royal houses recognise a High Sovereign; Urakai clans are capable political actors. - Valtorian mobilisation near Aldermere and increasing Karak-Varn eastern-garrison recruitment are current reports, not a confirmed war. - Edrik Voss's claim that King Durgan IV has not been informed of the eastern-mine activity is unverified. Lord Chancellor Veyron's motives and the royal government's actual knowledge remain open. - Royal Mining Office records, guard actions and restricted historical access can have ordinary institutional explanations; do not infer conspiracy by narrative convenience. - Religion, dissent, guilds, medicine, legal institutions, the economy and military logistics belong to living societies; do not invent a universally accepted pantheon, active rebellion or uniform administrative system. - Original Bible specifics worth retaining: religious traditions can include household rites, ancestor veneration, burial rites, charitable or educational institutions, religious law and nonreligious people. Military forces have regional differences in ranks, training, pay, recruitment and veteran lives. These are possibility frameworks, not a filled-out list of named institutions. Direct source: Politics, Factions & Institutions. Historical source: The Eryndor World Bible. --- ## Regional cultures and subcultures — new complete living-culture expansion Explicit creator rule: Every intelligent people has multiple cultures; every region contains overlapping local subcultures. The distinctive Khazari idea that contribution earns respect is not a generic value imposed on Eldar, Urakai, Halflings, Centaurs, Merfolk, Goblins or other peoples. Each community has its own admired paths, kinship traditions, duties, taboos and dissenting individuals. Culture comes from species + continent + settlement + state + occupation + household + life experience, and shared multi-species village identity can override older labels. 1. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas VIII — Thrones, Eldar, Urakai, Humans & Elder Courts: Seven independent Khazari traditions, multiple Eldar/Urakai branches, five human power-group subcultures, Drakari and Aelwyn courts. 2. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas IX — Smaller Peoples & Regional Traditions: Halflings, Gnomes, Goblins, Ents, Centaurs, Merfolk, Giants, the nine later-established peoples, and guarded unknowns for Living Mountains. 3. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas X — Animal Peoples, Diasporas & Mixed Communities: Wolvenkin, Foxfolk, Lionfolk, Tigerfolk, Elephantfolk, Bearfolk, Cowfolk and Pigfolk, all with several regional alternatives. 4. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas XI — All Peoples by Continent & Regional Subcultures: 28 modeled peoples × 5 continents regional crosswalk, 28 distinct cultural zones among five continents, shared mixed-town and professional subcultures, and methods for generating persistent local variation. Authority: These are new, creator-revisable setting expansions, not recovered original history or dialogue. Old confirmed ethnic/political foundations and Gloin's story take priority. No birth rates, marriage ratios, offspring biology, family sizes, lifespans or population totals change. Big families and centuries-long craft pursuits coexist, and no NPC gains world knowledge automatically. Current in-game time remains Autumn Day 22, Year 3,847, 11:25 AM. ## Newly created regional rulers, institutions and autonomous factions Eryndor Living Atlas II — Avarra, Seven Thrones & Regional Settlements adds proposed houses and ruling sovereigns for the six previously unnamed Mountain Thrones while preserving King Durgan IV of Karak-Varn and their political independence. Eryndor Living Atlas V — Factions, Mercenaries, Adventures & Gloin's Travel describes mercenary companies, independent adventuring groups, political trade institutions, lawful and unlawful actors and the routes Gloin might later choose. New setting expansion, not recovered original transcript. None of these additional groups is assumed responsible for the current sealed-mine mysteries, missing engineers, the unseen Urakai warlord or the elven prince. ## Complete topic reference — preserved from the preceding edition Eryndor's societies contain governments, royal courts, councils, noble houses, guilds, religious institutions, scholarly orders, military organisations, merchant families and local authorities. These institutions have their own interests, internal divisions, rivalries and histories. They are not one unified power structure, and no institution should be treated as automatically benevolent, corrupt or omniscient. ## Original Age of Crowns opening situation — Year 3,847 The creator's recovered original campaign-opening brief established an uneasy peace known as the Concord of Crowns, maintained by the great powers for nearly two centuries. This is a named historical-political context, not proof that every state was at peace or that any particular treaty term has been documented. At the campaign's start the great powers faced six simultaneous developments: 1. Valtorian Empire: military mobilisation along its northern frontier, with the Day 19 Karak-Varn intelligence item specifically placing troops near Aldermere's frontier. A war had not yet been established. 2. Letharion: an elven prince was reported missing. Separately, the elven court requested an audience with King Durgan IV. Do not assume the diplomatic request and disappearance had the same cause. 3. Dwarven mountain holds: three holds had stopped communicating with one another. The three were not individually named in the recovered brief; do not equate them automatically to three of the Seven Great Mountain Thrones. 4. Urakai: clans were gathering beneath a new warlord; that individual's name, aims and extent of authority were not specified. 5. Drakari: a dragon was reportedly seen above human territory for the first time in 400 years; the account did not identify the dragon or prove that no other covert sightings occurred. 6. Southern desert: something ancient was reportedly stirring. Its nature and relationship to other events were expressly unknown. The campaign's Day 19 world-intelligence notices also recorded rising iron prices linked to demand for military-grade iron and a Royal Mining Office silence about the mine closure. Treat these as starting-world conditions and reports; Gloin was not automatically personally informed of every event, and the six developments were not known to be connected. Local institutional detail from the recovered Day 19 scenes: The Royal Army advertised a three-year initial infantry enlistment with wages, crown-supplied equipment, training, barracks and meals. A Crownward recruitment office was said to be around twenty minutes from Borin's alehouse. Gloin considered enlistment but did not enlist in the recovered 7:20–9:35 AM sequence. Edrik Voss later claimed crown authorisation for a survey request and attributed mine-investigation supervision to Lord Chancellor Veyron; the authenticity and scope of this authority and the King's actual knowledge remain unverified. ## Political principles - Political power is distributed among kingdoms, thrones, courts, councils, city authorities, clans, confederations, guilds and other institutions. - Institutions can have independent agendas and internal factions. Their members may disagree about policy, methods and loyalties. - Personal motives and institutional interests can overlap without being identical. - A ruler's orders do not automatically represent every official or subordinate's intentions. - Rumours, accusations and claims of secret activity must be treated as evidence of what someone said, not proof that the claim is true. - Diplomacy, trade, treaties, rivalries and alliances can coexist. Political opponents may still trade or negotiate. - Institutions should have practical responsibilities, resources, limits, internal procedures and competing priorities. ## The Seven Khazari Mountain Thrones The Khazari are organised among seven powerful, culturally distinct and politically independent mountain thrones. They share deep traditions of mining, engineering, craftsmanship and runic work, but are not one uniform kingdom. The names, rulers, populations, alliances, laws and diplomatic relationships of all seven thrones have not yet been fully recorded. Do not invent details for the six less-developed thrones as if they were already established. ### Karak-Varn Karak-Varn is one of the Seven Thrones. - Ruler: King Durgan IV Stonehand. - King's age: 214. - Reign: 86 years. - Approximate population: 3.8 million. - Political character: Royal seat with administrative, military, industrial and civic institutions. - Relevant institutions: Royal court, military council, Royal Mining Office, Royal Historical Archive, craft guilds and the Iron Circle training complex. King Durgan IV is the reigning monarch. The existence of the royal court and military council is established; detailed membership, legal powers, succession procedures and internal factions need to be developed only when relevant. ## Other major powers ### Eldar of Letharion The Eldar civilisation has several royal houses gathered under a High Sovereign in the western forests of Letharion. Its full constitutional structure, house names, succession rules, court offices and military arrangements remain to be detailed. Eldar diplomatic culture is widely reputed for elaborate etiquette, exact language, formal precedence and refined political expression. This is a cultural reputation, not proof that all Eldar diplomats behave identically. ### Urakai confederations The Urakai are organised in clan confederations across eastern plains and highlands. They are a sophisticated and rising civilisation. Their ancient rivalry with the Khazari is political, territorial, industrial and military. Trade and alliances remain possible. Individual clans, confederation structures, leadership titles, councils, treaties and succession customs have not yet been fully specified. ### Human powers The five major human groupings have distinct broad political reputations and interests: - Aldermere: Duty-bound, practical and community-minded; values loyalty, courage and keeping one's word. - Valtoria: Disciplined, hierarchical, ambitious and politically calculating; values order, military achievement, status and national strength. - Northern Holds: Hardy and cautious with outsiders until trust is earned; values kinship, hospitality, endurance and survival. - Merchant Republics: Commercially minded and cosmopolitan; negotiation, wealth, opportunity and information are important sources of influence. - Southern Sultanates: Culturally sophisticated, scholarly and politically experienced; trade, ceremony, reputation, learning and hospitality matter. The exact constitutions, rulers, city-states, noble houses, councils and treaties of these powers remain open for development. ## Institutions across Eryndor The following types of institutions exist as part of the established world framework. Specific names, memberships, structures and jurisdiction should be recorded when they are actually established. ### Royal councils and courts Rulers may rely on councils, ministers, chancellors, advisers, judges, military commanders and household officials. Different courts may divide authority in different ways. A royal council is not necessarily unanimous, and court access does not prove that an adviser controls the ruler. ### Noble houses and political families Noble houses may control land, fortifications, trade privileges, military obligations, mines, roads or court offices. Their power may derive from inheritance, wealth, service, alliances, marriage, religious standing or historical claims. Houses can compete internally as well as with one another. Do not invent a noble genealogy or claim of succession without establishing it. ### Guilds and craft institutions Guilds may regulate apprenticeships, standards, work rights, prices, access to materials, trade privileges and professional disputes. They can support members while also protecting monopolies or resisting outside competition. Khazari craft and industrial life includes specialist workshops and professional traditions. The specific guild structure of every city remains to be developed. ### Merchant families and commercial powers Merchant families, trading houses, banks, shipping interests, caravan operators and market authorities can influence politics through credit, supply contracts, access to goods, tolls and information. Their interests may cross borders and sometimes rival those of rulers. ### Mage colleges and scholarly orders Mage colleges, libraries, historical societies, runic schools, scholarly orders and specialist archives exist as possible and accepted institutional forms in Eryndor's wider world. They may regulate research, train practitioners, preserve dangerous knowledge or compete for discoveries. Their particular names, jurisdictions, doctrines, admission rules and political power remain open unless individually established. Not every scholar belongs to a college, and not every magical tradition is centrally regulated. ### Military orders and royal guards Eryndor's military institutions may include standing armies, militias, elite units, royal guards, military orders, naval forces, academies and specialist corps. They have ranks, logistics, training, supply chains, fortifications and command structures. Their quality and organisation vary by state. The existence of elite troops does not mean every army is professional or uniformly equipped. ### Local government and public authority Towns, cities, ports, mining settlements and rural districts may have officials responsible for law, public works, taxes, markets, safety, water, roads and local disputes. The level of autonomy varies by region and ruler. ## Religion, belief and spiritual institutions Eryndor has religious and spiritual traditions across its peoples and regions. The broad world framework includes: - Pantheons and local deities. - Temples, shrines and priesthoods. - Sacred sites, pilgrimage routes and festivals. - Competing histories, doctrines and interpretations. - Heresies, reform movements, cults and dissident traditions. - Religious orders and institutions that may wield social, political or economic influence. Belief is not automatically objective truth. A faith may be socially powerful and sincerely held without every historical claim or supernatural doctrine being confirmed. Different religions may explain the same event differently. Some sacred traditions may preserve genuine historical knowledge; others may be symbolic, contested or mistaken. No complete pantheon, universal theology or list of named deities has been established in this reference. Do not invent one as though it were already canon. ## Military and strategic affairs The world framework includes: - Standing armies and local militias. - Elite military units and specialist forces. - Navies and maritime powers. - Military academies, training grounds and rank systems. - Supply, logistics, transport and engineering. - Fortresses, walls, gates, siege equipment and defensive works. - Royal guards and military orders. - Contracts, mercenaries, scouts, guides and adventuring companies. Military strength depends on training, command, logistics, morale, equipment, terrain, money and political cohesion. A technologically advanced army is not automatically invincible. Mobilisation and military recruitment create costs and political consequences. ## Dissent, resistance and rebellion Political dissent, organised opposition, civil unrest, resistance and rebellion are natural possibilities in Eryndor. No kingdom, throne, confederation, republic, court or institution is assumed to be universally obedient or politically stable. Forms of dissent may include: - Civic opposition: petitions, public criticism, demonstrations, organised campaigns, strikes, boycotts and demands for reform. - Economic unrest: labour disputes, guild conflicts, tax resistance, food riots, debt protests, disputes over tolls and opposition to monopolies. - Political factionalism: rival ministers, councils, noble houses, guild interests, regional leaders and court factions competing for influence or policy. - Regional resistance: communities resisting central authority, outside administration, conscription, resource extraction, cultural assimilation or loss of local privileges. - Religious dissent: reform movements, rival interpretations, challenges to religious authorities, sectarian conflict or resistance to state interference in belief. - Military dissent: mutiny, refusal of unlawful orders, rival command loyalties, veteran movements, coups or military-backed political challenges. - Separatism and rebellion: attempts to win autonomy, restore a former ruler, replace a government, establish a new state or overthrow an existing order. Working principles: - Dissent is not automatically treason, and rebellion is not automatically righteous. Motives, grievances, methods and public support vary. - Opposition movements should have understandable causes, internal disagreements, leadership, resources, supporters, opponents and practical limitations. - Movements may be peaceful, constitutional, clandestine, violent or change form over time. - Not every grievance produces rebellion. Governments may negotiate, reform, repress, ignore, divide or accommodate opposition; communities may tolerate hardship for many reasons. - Rebellions require more than anger. Organisation, leadership, money, supplies, communications, weapons, safe territory, public legitimacy and opportunities all matter. - Different political systems produce different forms of opposition. A merchant republic, hereditary monarchy, clan confederation and council-governed city should not all experience dissent in the same way. - Foreign powers may support, exploit, undermine or oppose internal movements, but outside involvement must be established through evidence rather than assumed. - Political conflict has consequences for civilians, trade, security, law, migration, military deployments and the economy. The potential for dissent and rebellion is established across Eryndor. Specific factions, grievances, leaders, programmes, levels of popular support and current unrest remain open until developed. This framework does not itself establish an active rebellion, rebel leader or secret conspiracy. ## Current political context — campaign-era reports The following conditions are established as the political backdrop around Gloin's current campaign period. They are not a full political chronology and should be updated only when new events are established. ### Avarran frontier and military posture - Valtoria is mobilising forces near Aldermere's northern frontier. - Scouts have reportedly been seen near the frontier. - Karak-Varn's military council is expanding recruitment for the eastern garrison. - Military demand is contributing to rising iron prices. These developments create regional tension, but do not by themselves establish that a war has begun or that either side intends an immediate invasion. ### Letharion and Karak-Varn The Eldar court of Letharion has requested an audience with King Durgan IV. The precise purpose, agenda, diplomatic stakes and outcome of the requested audience are not yet established. ### Eastern mine investigation and political authority - Lord Chancellor Veyron is handling the eastern mine investigation privately. - Edrik Voss, Deputy Examiner of the Royal Mining Office, said that King Durgan IV had not been informed. - Edrik's statement is a reported claim, not independently verified proof of the King's ignorance. - Two miners at the Copper Kettle were overheard saying equipment was moving towards the old eastern access and Royal Mining Office guards had doubled. This is an unverified rumour, not an established movement of equipment or confirmed increase in guard strength. - There is no established proof of a conspiracy or of deliberate wrongdoing by the Crown, the Royal Mining Office or the Chancellor. Keep the distinction between restricted procedures, institutional caution, political disagreement and actual conspiracy. Do not treat secrecy alone as proof of guilt. The rumours do not establish that war has begun, that an invasion is imminent, or that the eastern mine reports are true. ## Institutional development checklist When a specific institution becomes relevant, establish: - Its name, location, purpose and history. - Who holds authority and how they obtained it. - Its formal responsibilities and actual influence. - Its membership, ranks, resources and internal factions. - Its laws, customs, rituals, fees or procedures. - Its allies, rivals and political dependencies. - What it knows, what it believes, and what it is concealing or misunderstanding. - How it affects ordinary people, trade, law, security and daily life. Keep these details consistent across the relevant characters, geography, history and campaign records. ## Wider society and everyday institutions Eryndor's societies should function as recognisable, complex civilisations. Many institutions resemble familiar social structures, even where technology, customs and political systems differ. Develop practical details when they matter rather than making ordinary life needlessly exotic simply because the setting is fantasy. Relevant systems include: - Law courts, policing, prisons, contracts, property rights and local government. - Schools, universities, apprenticeships, libraries, medicine and public health. - Banks, credit, insurance, taxation, customs, wages and veteran support. - Roads, bridges, ports, postal and messenger services, public works and sanitation. - Farmers, craftspeople, labourers, merchants, professionals, landlords and the organisations that represent or regulate them. - News, public notices, rumour networks, printing and other systems for circulating information. - Family life, marriage, inheritance, housing, leisure, sport, entertainment and festivals. The form and availability of these systems varies by region, wealth, population, technology and government. Do not assume every settlement has every institution, or that all societies organise them in the same way.
